MANILA, Philippines — The local stock market snapped its three-day winning streak as investors stayed on the sidelines due to a lack of fresh leads.
The benchmark Philippine Stock Exchange index slipped by 0.06 percent, or 3.28 points, to close the session at 5,490.13.
The broader All Shares index also inched down by 0.03 percent or 0.94 points, settling at 3,052.97.
“The Philippine equity space pared intraday losses to finish nearly unchanged, as investors consolidated gains from the market’s three-session rebound ahead of Friday’s MSCI rebalancing and month-end positioning,” First Metro Securities said.
Philstocks Financial Inc. said trading was lethargic, implying that many chose to stay on the sidelines amid lingering uncertainties.
“Overall, the market is seen to be in a cautious mood, as investors deal with risks to our economic outlook, primarily stagflation risks, while waiting for new catalysts,” Philstocks Financial said.
Sectors were a mixed bag, with those in the green having the slight advantage. Mining and oil posted the biggest increase at 0.87 percent, while services lost the most at 0.84 percent.
Total value turnover expanded to P21.09 billion from the previous day’s P7.9 billion.
Foreigners were net sellers with net outflows of P252.77 million.
“Offshore investors reversed their midday buying stance to finish with P252.77 million in net outflows, extending their selling streak to a fifth consecutive session,” First Metro Securities said.
Decliners crushed advancers, 94 to 79, while 63 issues were unchanged.
ICTSI was the session’s top traded stock, shedding 1.28 percent to P770 per share. It was followed by Meralco and SM Investments, which climbed by 3.73 percent and 0.62 percent, respectively, to P395.20 and P571.

article.text:
Philippine financial markets ended trading on Thursday in the red, with the local stock barometer snapping a three-day winning streak and the peso depreciating slightly against the greenback on rising global oil prices and geopolitical tensions.
The geopolitical tensions partly dragged the Philippine peso, which shed 4.5 centavos to close Thursday at P63.72:$1 from Wednesday’s finish of P63.675:$1.
“The US dollar/peso exchange rate corrected slightly higher after recent signals of less aggressive monetary tightening/rate hikes by the BSP amid softer local economic growth; also after global crude oil prices went up to new one-week highs,” Rizal Commercial Banking Corp. (RCBC) chief economist Michael Ricafort said in a mobile message.
The main Philippine Stock Exchange index (PSEi) lost 3.28 points or 0.06% to 5,490.13. The broader All Shares index declined by 0.94 points or 0.03% to 3,052.97.
BSP airs concern over PH's declining foreign reserves
Marcos rejects call to reassess economic team amid 'malaise'
“The PSEi corrected slightly lower after global crude oil prices went up to new one-week highs amid Iran-backed Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, several vessels hit Iranian mines in the Straight of Hormuz recently,” Ricafort said.
Yemen's Houthi rebels on Wednesday warned that they would target the Saudi port of Jeddah and other ports along the Red Sea coast if Saudi Arabia attacks Yemen's port of Hodeidah.
Brent crude traded $2.20 or 2.41% higher at $93.60 per barrel as of 10:16 a.m. ET, while West Texas Intermediate gained $1.46 ot 1.78% to $83.51.
Most indices closed positively — financials up 0.36%, industrial by 0.03%, holding firms by 0.67%, and mining and oil by 0.87%. The property index fell by 0.59%, and services by 0.84%.
More than 2.317 billion shares, valued at P21.085 billion, changed hands. Decliners led advancers, 94 to 79, while 63 issues were unchanged.
BSP governor Eli Remolona Jr. earlier this week said a pause on monetary policy tightening is possible but unlikely, while maintaining that the prolonged economic weakness may have lessened the case for aggressive rate hikes.
Ricafort also cited new taxes announced by US President Donald Trump, who proposed levies on 14 trading partners — the highest of which would be a 20% rate on China — for Thursday’s depreciation.
“Nevertheless, the peso still posted a net appreciation vs. the US dollar for nearly a month already since President Marcos gave signals of reassurance on the peso exchange rate since October 28, 2026,” Ricafort said. —LDF, GMA News

deepDives.title: PH has less room to support growth
deepDives.summary: THE Philippines is becoming increasingly vulnerable to a combination of rising global borrowing costs and higher energy prices, with tighter financial conditions and mounting inflation pressures leaving policymakers with less room to support economic growth, an international bank said in a report on Thursday.ANZ Research, the economic and financial markets research division of the Australia and N…
reasons: reader relevance 2/3: Energy prices and borrowing costs pressure the economy
promoted to deep dive in place of "Pag-IBIG shifts to electronic disbursement for loa"

article.text:
THE Philippines is becoming increasingly vulnerable to a combination of rising global borrowing costs and higher energy prices, with tighter financial conditions and mounting inflation pressures leaving policymakers with less room to support economic growth, an international bank said in a report on Thursday.
ANZ Research, the economic and financial markets research division of the Australia and New Zealand Banking Group (ANZ), identified the Philippines, alongside India, Indonesia and Thailand, as particularly exposed to the simultaneous pressures because of their dependence on imported energy and limited participation in the global artificial intelligence (AI) investment boom.
The bank said the global investment shift toward the United States had made it more difficult for emerging Asian economies to attract foreign capital, while higher energy prices were adding to inflation, weakening external balances and straining government finances.
“With inflation rising, external buffers weakening and US real rates likely to remain high, policymakers have progressively less room to keep domestic financial conditions supportive,” ANZ Research said.
“For the region’s energy importers, especially outside the AI cycle, protecting nominal stability may increasingly have to take precedence over protecting currently strong growth,” it added.
While economic growth across nearly all Asian economies outside China has held up better than expected despite the challenging global environment, ANZ warned that the combination of these shocks could make conditions more difficult in the coming months.
“Higher energy prices raise inflation, weaken energy importers’ current accounts and strain fiscal positions when governments try to cushion households,” ANZ said.
“At the same time, higher US rates make low Asian real rates harder to sustain without putting pressure on currencies and capital flows,” it added.
It argued that this combination had left policymakers with “less room to support growth while containing inflation and preserving external stability.”
ANZ said the Philippines was particularly vulnerable because, unlike technology-oriented economies benefiting from the AI investment boom, its investment activity was being held back by policy constraints.
South Korea and Taiwan have benefited from their exposure to semiconductors, memory chips and AI hardware, while Malaysia and Singapore have also participated in the technology upswing because of their positions in the semiconductor supply chain.
The Philippines, however, has not enjoyed the same investment momentum.
ANZ estimated that gross investment accounts for around 32 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in India, 30 percent in Indonesia and 25 percent in Thailand, and noted that investment had strengthened in several regional economies through domestic fiscal support and spending in selected sectors.
“The Philippines is an exception, as policy stasis is holding back investment,” the bank said.
The divergence leaves the country more exposed to external shocks, particularly as global investors increasingly favor US assets offering stronger corporate returns and higher yields.
The bank said stronger corporate returns in the United States and increasingly attractive yields had drawn global funds toward American markets, making emerging-market investments less competitive.
The trend is expected to persist as AI-related financing requirements remain elevated.
“India, Indonesia and the Philippines offer higher yields than the regional average, but their carry advantage diminishes once higher returns elsewhere and FX-hedging costs are considered,” ANZ said.
ANZ also warned that inflation buffers across the region had weakened, leaving several economies more exposed to additional price increases.
It noted that Philippines was already recording inflation above its tolerance range, while South Korea had also moved above its upper boundary.
Consumer price growth has remained above the 2.0- to 4.0-percent target of the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) since the Middle East war started in March.
Inflation hit 7.8 percent in October and BSP Governor Eli Remolona Jr. said it could hit 8.0 percent in the coming months due to lingering impact of the energy crisis and looming El Niño.
This creates a difficult policy environment for central banks, which must balance the need to support domestic demand against the risks of currency depreciation and accelerating inflation.
ANZ noted that real policy interest rates, measured using three-month average inflation, remained below zero in India, Indonesia and Malaysia and were around zero in South Korea.
The Philippines and Thailand are the only economies in the group with clearly positive real policy rates.
“Muted real-rate adjustment was defensible while inflation was weak, as it let central banks cushion domestic demand rather than directly import tighter US financial conditions,” ANZ said.
“The cost has been heavier reliance on currencies to absorb the divergence, leaving policymakers balancing growth against FX pressure, often through extraordinary regulatory measures,” it added.
The BSP policymaking body Monetary Board raised key policy rates by a total of 125 basis points since April to contain rising inflation. This brought key policy rates at 5.5 percent.

MANILA, Philippines — Full year economic growth may still reach three percent this year, but getting there is a big challenge amid risks including high inflation, according to the Department of Economy, Planning and Development (DEPDev).
Speaking to reporters, DEPDev Secretary Arsenio Balisacan said that a three-percent growth remains possible for this year, but would entail posting faster growth in the current quarter.
If realized, a three-percent growth this year would fall below the government’s 3.5 to 4.5 percent growth goal for the year.
From January to September, the economy grew by an average of 2.5 percent, also lower than the growth target for this year.
In the third quarter alone, the economy grew by 2.1 percent, the slowest since 2021, amid high inflation, lower agricultural output and weak investments.
“So we need to grow a little bit more in the fourth quarter to get close as much as possible to three (percent),” Balisacan said.
“It’s tough, because to get to the three or 3.5 (percent), which is the lower end of the (target) range, we need to grow something like six percent, which at the current situation is quite a big challenge,” he said.
If international crude oil prices, which are now back at the $80 level could go down further, he said it would be a big boost for the country.
The Middle East conflict involving the United States, Israel and Iran that started in late February, triggered an oil shock, pushing up prices of fuel and other goods and weighing on consumption.
The Philippine economy was hit hard by the crisis as it relies on the Middle East for its oil imports and consumption serves as its main growth driver.
Given the latest economic performance and ongoing uncertainty, Balisacan said that the Development Budget Coordination Committee is set to review the growth targets next month.
Rizal Commercial Banking Corp. chief economist Michael Ricafort said in an email that a possible catch-up in government spending on infrastructure would still support a possible average gross domestic product (GDP) growth of three percent levels for 2026.
“Passage of priority reform measures especially on better leveling up governance standards such as the anti-political dynasty bill, reforming the party-list system, CADENA Bill, creation of an independent people’s commission, other anti-corruption measures, fiscal reforms and other economic reform measures would help improve sentiment or confidence of investors, some of which on the sidelines since the anomalous flood-control projects were exposed in the latter part of 2025,” he said.
For his part, Pantheon Macroeconomics chief emerging Asia economist Miguel Chanco said in an email that he expects only a small recovery in GDP growth this quarter to 2.3 percent.
“It will be a while, from my vantage point, before GDP growth will be able to rise more meaningfully, particularly as consumption and investment are struggling to build and maintain any real positive momentum, for a host of reasons, including the weakness of household balance sheets and subdued consumer and business confidence,” he said.

MANILA, Philippines — The Home Development Mutual Fund or Pag-IBIG Fund reported a 55-percent increase in the number of homes secured by Filipino families through its Acquired Assets Program as of end-October.
Latest data released by Pag-IBIG showed that there were 18,071 homes secured by Filipino homebuyers in the January-to-October period, up from 11,664 homes in the same period last year.
These properties had a combined sales value of P25.23 billion, a 74 percent increase from P14.53 billion in the same period last year, with an average purchase price of approximately P1.40 million per property.
Pag-IBIG CEO Marilene Acosta said the program provides members with another avenue to homeownership through discounted properties and affordable financing options.
“With the discounts we offer and our affordable financing options, members can find homes that suit their needs and budgets, whether they are looking for their first home or seeking to finally own the property where their families have been living,” Acosta said.
Pag-IBIG is offering discounts of up to 30 percent on its acquired properties nationwide through its ongoing Acquired Assets Super Sale Part 2, which runs until Dec. 31.
The second installment builds on the success of the first Super Sale, launched in August 2025.
“Every home acquired through this program also enables us to recover funds that we can use to finance more homes for our members, while generating earnings that help us grow the savings of our entire membership through annual dividends,” Acosta said.
Qualified buyers may purchase the properties through cash, short-term installment arrangements or Pag-IBIG housing loans, which offer repayment periods of up to 30 years.
Meanwhile, Department of Human Settlements and Urban Development Secretary Jose Ramon Aliling said the program is among the diverse housing modalities under the Expanded Pambansang Pabahay para sa Pilipino (Expanded 4PH) Program.
“Our comprehensive approach under Expanded 4PH goes beyond expanding the supply of new homes,” Aliling said, who also chairs the Pag-IBIG Board.
“It also includes making existing housing inventory more accessible and affordable through programs such as Pag-IBIG Fund’s Acquired Assets, one of the many housing options we are making available to Filipino families,” he added.
Pag-IBIG also offers its Lease with Option to Purchase Program to qualified occupants of its Acquired Assets who are not yet financially ready to purchase the properties they occupy.
The program allows occupants to legitimize their tenure through a lease arrangement while providing a pathway toward eventual ownership of their homes.
The state-run firm said interested homebuyers may explore available properties, create their buyer ID and participate in online bidding through the Acquired Assets section of the official Pag-IBIG website.
Pag-IBIG booked a net income of P63.23 billion in the January-to-September period, up 23.5 percent from P51.19 billion in the same period last year.

related.title: BOC speeds up cargo release, removes prior IAS clearance

article.text:
The Bureau of Customs (BOC) has issued a memorandum that removes the mandatory prior clearance from the Imports Assessment Service (IAS) for select imports to speed up cargo release.
OCOM Memorandum Order No. 124-2026 removes the IAS clearance required for automobiles and other motor vehicles, heavy equipment and other machinery, brand-new and used buses, and brand-new trucks. It also covers ships, boats and other floating structures, iron and steel (including bulk and break-bulk shipments), bulk rice, and resin.
“Our goal is to bring down the cost of doing business in the country. For importers, this reform could reduce cargo processing time by around 3-5 days. That means faster movement of goods and lower logistics costs," said Customs Commissioner Charlito Mendoza in a statement.
Further, BOC officers at the ports will continue to verify the description, tariff classification, and customs value of imported goods and determine the duties and taxes due.

Sen. Alan Cayetano wants us Filipinos to emulate Koreans in helping government repay its debts. He took Political Science as pre-Law course. He should thus contextualize why Koreans in 1998 donated household jewelry and gold to their government to help avert foreign debt default.
Koreans at that time were in high spirits. Two corrupt presidents, Chun Doo-hwan and Roh Tae-woo, had just been convicted. Reforms were underway. Korea’s future looked bright.
It was the second time Koreans bailed out their government. In 1907 they donated cash, land and jewelry to pay off Korea’s national debt to Japan. Japan was then threatening to annex Korea, which it did through other means in 1910.

We live in an era obsessed with disruption, optimization, and reform. Walk into any boardroom, government hall, or civic assembly, and the loudest applause is reserved for the self-proclaimed “fixer” – the leader who arrives with a binder of new policies, a mandate to overhaul the system, and an urgent desire to set things right.
In truth, reformers are celebrated because their work is visible, measurable, and dramatic. Yet, behind many well-intentioned crusades lies a quiet flaw: a servant leader is not a reformist.
The difference is not merely semantic; it is existential. It lies in what the leader sees when they look at the room.
When a reformist looks at an institution or a nation, they see a broken machine. Their instinct is diagnosis and correction. In their urgency to repair systems, streamline processes, and hit targets, people subtly become variables in an equation—obstacles…

The brouhaha over the approval of House Bill (HB) 10858, otherwise known as the 2027 General Appropriations Bill (GAB), apparently triggered loose talks about leadership change in the Lower Chamber. Abiding by tradition at the House of Representatives, Speaker Faustino “Bojie” Dy lll is identified as the principal author of the House-approved 2027 GAB while the chairperson of the House committee on appropriations, Nueva Ecija Rep. Mikaela Suansing, and the rest of Congress members who voted “Yes” are co-authors.
The 2027 GAB was approved by 282 votes in favor, 13 against and one abstention. The House-approved 2027 GAB triggered serious concerns even among pro-administration members of the 20th Congress.
